search_paper_list.title:
Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of
  ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews
search_paper_list.summary:
We present an approach for estimating the fraction of text in a large corpus
which is likely to be substantially modified or produced by a large language
model (LLM). Our maximum likelihood model leverages expert-written and
AI-generated reference texts to accurately and efficiently examine real-world
LLM-use at the corpus level. We apply this approach to a case study of
scientific peer review in AI conferences that took place after the release of
ChatGPT: ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023. Our results suggest
that between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these
conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs, i.e. beyond
spell-checking or minor writing updates. The circumstances in which generated
text occurs offer insight into user behavior: the estimated fraction of
LLM-generated text is higher in reviews which report lower confidence, were
submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to
respond to author rebuttals. We also observe corpus-level trends in generated
text which may be too subtle to detect at the individual level, and discuss the
implications of such trends on peer review. We call for future
interdisciplinary work to examine how LLM use is changing our information and
knowledge practices.

search_paper_list.title:
Evoke: Evoking Critical Thinking Abilities in LLMs via Reviewer-Author
  Prompt Editing
search_paper_list.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have made impressive progress in natural
language processing. These models rely on proper human instructions (or
prompts) to generate suitable responses. However, the potential of LLMs are not
fully harnessed by commonly-used prompting methods: many human-in-the-loop
algorithms employ ad-hoc procedures for prompt selection; while auto prompt
generation approaches are essentially searching all possible prompts randomly
and inefficiently. We propose Evoke, an automatic prompt refinement framework.
In Evoke, there are two instances of a same LLM: one as a reviewer
(LLM-Reviewer), it scores the current prompt; the other as an author
(LLM-Author), it edits the prompt by considering the edit history and the
reviewer's feedback. Such an author-reviewer feedback loop ensures that the
prompt is refined in each iteration. We further aggregate a data selection
approach to Evoke, where only the hard samples are exposed to the LLM. The hard
samples are more important because the LLM can develop deeper understanding of
the tasks out of them, while the model may already know how to solve the easier
cases. Experimental results show that Evoke significantly outperforms existing
methods. For instance, in the challenging task of logical fallacy detection,
Evoke scores above 80, while all other baseline methods struggle to reach 20.

search_paper_list.title:
The AI Review Lottery: Widespread AI-Assisted Peer Reviews Boost Paper
  Scores and Acceptance Rates
search_paper_list.summary:
Journals and conferences worry that peer reviews assisted by artificial
intelligence (AI), in particular, large language models (LLMs), may negatively
influence the validity and fairness of the peer-review system, a cornerstone of
modern science. In this work, we address this concern with a quasi-experimental
study of the prevalence and impact of AI-assisted peer reviews in the context
of the 2024 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), a
large and prestigious machine-learning conference. Our contributions are
threefold. Firstly, we obtain a lower bound for the prevalence of AI-assisted
reviews at ICLR 2024 using the GPTZero LLM detector, estimating that at least
$15.8\%$ of reviews were written with AI assistance. Secondly, we estimate the
impact of AI-assisted reviews on submission scores. Considering pairs of
reviews with different scores assigned to the same paper, we find that in
$53.4\%$ of pairs the AI-assisted review scores higher than the human review
($p = 0.002$; relative difference in probability of scoring higher: $+14.4\%$
in favor of AI-assisted reviews). Thirdly, we assess the impact of receiving an
AI-assisted peer review on submission acceptance. In a matched study,
submissions near the acceptance threshold that received an AI-assisted peer
review were $4.9$ percentage points ($p = 0.024$) more likely to be accepted
than submissions that did not. Overall, we show that AI-assisted reviews are
consequential to the peer-review process and offer a discussion on future
implications of current trends

search_paper_list.title:
Bias-Free Estimation in Multicomponent Maximum Likelihood Fits with
  Component-Dependent Templates
search_paper_list.summary:
The possibility of strong biases in a multicomponent Maximum Likelihood fits
with component-dependent templates has been demonstrated in some toy problems.
We discuss here in detail a problem of practical interest, particle
identification based on time-of-flight or dE/dx information. We show that large
biases can occur in estimating particle fractions in a sample if differences
between the momentum spectra of particles are ignored, and we present a more
robust fit technique, allowing bias-free estimation even when the particle
spectra in the sample are unknown.

search_paper_list.title:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation is All You Need for Well-Specified
  Covariate Shift
search_paper_list.summary:
A key challenge of modern machine learning systems is to achieve
Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization -- generalizing to target data whose
distribution differs from that of source data. Despite its significant
importance, the fundamental question of ``what are the most effective
algorithms for OOD generalization'' remains open even under the standard
setting of covariate shift. This paper addresses this fundamental question by
proving that, surprisingly, classical Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
purely using source data (without any modification) achieves the minimax
optimality for covariate shift under the well-specified setting. That is, no
algorithm performs better than MLE in this setting (up to a constant factor),
justifying MLE is all you need. Our result holds for a very rich class of
parametric models, and does not require any boundedness condition on the
density ratio. We illustrate the wide applicability of our framework by
instantiating it to three concrete examples -- linear regression, logistic
regression, and phase retrieval. This paper further complement the study by
proving that, under the misspecified setting, MLE is no longer the optimal
choice, whereas Maximum Weighted Likelihood Estimator (MWLE) emerges as minimax
optimal in certain scenarios.

search_paper_list.title:
Theoretical Insights for Diffusion Guidance: A Case Study for Gaussian
  Mixture Models
search_paper_list.summary:
Diffusion models benefit from instillation of task-specific information into
the score function to steer the sample generation towards desired properties.
Such information is coined as guidance. For example, in text-to-image
synthesis, text input is encoded as guidance to generate semantically aligned
images. Proper guidance inputs are closely tied to the performance of diffusion
models. A common observation is that strong guidance promotes a tight alignment
to the task-specific information, while reducing the diversity of the generated
samples. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical study towards
understanding the influence of guidance on diffusion models in the context of
Gaussian mixture models. Under mild conditions, we prove that incorporating
diffusion guidance not only boosts classification confidence but also
diminishes distribution diversity, leading to a reduction in the differential
entropy of the output distribution. Our analysis covers the widely adopted
sampling schemes including DDPM and DDIM, and leverages comparison inequalities
for differential equations as well as the Fokker-Planck equation that
characterizes the evolution of probability density function, which may be of
independent theoretical interest.

search_paper_list.title: Transformers can optimally learn regression mixture models
search_paper_list.summary:
Mixture models arise in many regression problems, but most methods have seen
limited adoption partly due to these algorithms' highly-tailored and
model-specific nature. On the other hand, transformers are flexible, neural
sequence models that present the intriguing possibility of providing
general-purpose prediction methods, even in this mixture setting. In this work,
we investigate the hypothesis that transformers can learn an optimal predictor
for mixtures of regressions. We construct a generative process for a mixture of
linear regressions for which the decision-theoretic optimal procedure is given
by data-driven exponential weights on a finite set of parameters. We observe
that transformers achieve low mean-squared error on data generated via this
process. By probing the transformer's output at inference time, we also show
that transformers typically make predictions that are close to the optimal
predictor. Our experiments also demonstrate that transformers can learn
mixtures of regressions in a sample-efficient fashion and are somewhat robust
to distribution shifts. We complement our experimental observations by proving
constructively that the decision-theoretic optimal procedure is indeed
implementable by a transformer.

search_paper_list.title: Subtractive Mixture Models via Squaring: Representation and Learning
search_paper_list.summary:
Mixture models are traditionally represented and learned by adding several
distributions as components. Allowing mixtures to subtract probability mass or
density can drastically reduce the number of components needed to model complex
distributions. However, learning such subtractive mixtures while ensuring they
still encode a non-negative function is challenging. We investigate how to
learn and perform inference on deep subtractive mixtures by squaring them. We
do this in the framework of probabilistic circuits, which enable us to
represent tensorized mixtures and generalize several other subtractive models.
We theoretically prove that the class of squared circuits allowing subtractions
can be exponentially more expressive than traditional additive mixtures; and,
we empirically show this increased expressiveness on a series of real-world
distribution estimation tasks.

search_paper_list.title: Statistical Inference Under Constrained Selection Bias
search_paper_list.summary:
Large-scale datasets are increasingly being used to inform decision making.
While this effort aims to ground policy in real-world evidence, challenges have
arisen as selection bias and other forms of distribution shifts often plague
observational data. Previous attempts to provide robust inference have given
guarantees depending on a user-specified amount of possible distribution shift
(e.g., the maximum KL divergence between the observed and target
distributions). However, decision makers will often have additional knowledge
about the target distribution which constrains the kind of possible shifts. To
leverage such information, we propose a framework that enables statistical
inference in the presence of selection bias which obeys user-specified
constraints in the form of functions whose expectation is known under the
target distribution. The output is high-probability bounds on the value of an
estimand for the target distribution. Hence, our method leverages domain
knowledge in order to partially identify a wide class of estimands. We analyze
the computational and statistical properties of methods to estimate these
bounds and show that our method can produce informative bounds on a variety of
simulated and semisynthetic tasks, as well as in a real-world use case.

search_paper_list.title: Statistical Inference with Data Augmentation and Parameter Expansion
search_paper_list.summary:
Statistical pragmatism embraces all efficient methods in statistical
inference. Augmentation of the collected data is used herein to obtain
representative population information from a large class of non-representative
population's units. Parameter expansion of a probability model is shown to
reduce the upper bound on the sum of error probabilities for a test of simple
hypotheses, and a measure, R, is proposed for the effect of activating
additional component(s) in the sufficient statistic.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of
  ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
We present an approach for estimating the fraction of text in a large corpus
which is likely to be substantially modified or produced by a large language
model (LLM). Our maximum likelihood model leverages expert-written and
AI-generated reference texts to accurately and efficiently examine real-world
LLM-use at the corpus level. We apply this approach to a case study of
scientific peer review in AI conferences that took place after the release of
ChatGPT: ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023. Our results suggest
that between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these
conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs, i.e. beyond
spell-checking or minor writing updates. The circumstances in which generated
text occurs offer insight into user behavior: the estimated fraction of
LLM-generated text is higher in reviews which report lower confidence, were
submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to
respond to author rebuttals. We also observe corpus-level trends in generated
text which may be too subtle to detect at the individual level, and discuss the
implications of such trends on peer review. We call for future
interdisciplinary work to examine how LLM use is changing our information and
knowledge practices.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a computationally efficient framework to estimate the fraction (α) of AI-modified text in large corpora, specifically focusing on academic peer reviews. By modeling the review corpus as a mixture of human-written and AI-generated texts using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), the method is applied to evaluate changes in review quality and style post-ChatGPT release across major machine learning conferences.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach leverages historical data to create two reference distributions (P for human-written and Q for AI-generated texts) using token occurrence statistics (with a focus on adjectives, among other parts of speech). A mixture model is then established as (1 − α)P + αQ and maximum likelihood estimation is used to determine the fraction α. The methodology includes validation on synthetic mixtures and theoretical analysis showing the robustness and efficiency of the estimation.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on peer review datasets from major ML conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, EMNLP) as well as Nature portfolio journals. The setup involved generating AI-modified texts using LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 Chat, and Claude-2.1), creating synthetic mixtures with known proportions of AI-generated content, and comparing the MLE-based estimation against other instance-based detection methods. Extensive validation using bootstrap sampling and comparisons to baseline classifiers were performed, along with stratified analysis based on factors like submission deadlines and presence of scholarly citations.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The framework primarily focuses on detecting modifications from ChatGPT and similar models, which may not capture the full diversity of LLM outputs. It relies on simplifying assumptions such as representing documents based on token occurrence (e.g., adjectives) and may be sensitive to changes in style or prompt variations. Moreover, approximations in modeling the mixture and dependency on historical training data could introduce estimation errors and may not account for all nuances in human vs. AI writing styles.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could extend the framework to additional domains and other forms of AI-generated content beyond peer reviews, refine the methodology by incorporating different token types and deeper linguistic features, and address ethical and privacy concerns in using peer review data. There is also scope to improve robustness against prompt shifts, to explore fine-grained analysis at the document level, and to study long-term impacts on review quality and diversity in scholarly communication.

Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of
  ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
We present an approach for estimating the fraction of text in a large corpus
which is likely to be substantially modified or produced by a large language
model (LLM). Our maximum likelihood model leverages expert-written and
AI-generated reference texts to accurately and efficiently examine real-world
LLM-use at the corpus level. We apply this approach to a case study of

candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a novel, computationally efficient framework to estimate the proportion of text in large corpora that has been substantially modified or generated by large language models (LLMs). Using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) on a mixture model that combines human-written and AI-generated texts, the work presents a case study on AI conference peer reviews, revealing corpus‐level trends such as increases in AI-modifications after ChatGPT’s release and correlations with review characteristics (e.g., deadline effects, presence of citations, review confidence, and homogenization of feedback).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach parameterizes documents as collections of tokens (primarily adjectives) and models the text as being drawn from a mixture distribution ((1 − α)P + αQ), where P and Q represent the probability distributions of human-written and AI-generated text respectively. A maximum likelihood estimator is derived from the log-likelihood function L(α) = ∑ log((1 − α)P(x) + αQ(x)). Training data is generated by prompting an LLM with historical peer review instructions, and the method is validated using synthetic mixtures and sensitivity tests across different token types (adjectives, adverbs, verbs, nouns).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The experiments utilize large datasets from major machine learning conferences—ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, and EMNLP—as well as Nature Portfolio journals. The study employs synthetic validation setups where ground truth mixtures of human and AI-generated reviews are created. Benchmarks include comparing estimation errors to state-of-the-art instance-based detectors and exploring various factors (e.g., timing of review submission, citation usage, and reviewer confidence). Extensive sensitivity analyses, computational cost comparisons, and additional experiments (using alternative LLMs such as GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 Chat, and Claude-2.1) are conducted.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The study’s limitations include potential sensitivity to the choice of token vocabulary (e.g., adjectives vs. other parts of speech) and LLM prompting styles, as well as reliance on historical data that may be influenced by shifts in reviewers’ language or non-native speaker populations. Moreover, the framework abstracts text into aggregate statistics, which may miss finer instance-level differences, and the results may vary with the specific LLM used for generating training data. The method does not definitively detect individual AI-generated sentences but provides corpus-level estimates.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could extend the framework to other domains and publication venues, improve robustness against evolving LLM capabilities and prompt shifts, and further analyze the long-term impact of AI-generated modifications on scientific communication. Additional research is encouraged to explore improved token representations, individual-level detection methods, ethical implications in scholarly review systems, and integration with guidelines for responsible LLM usage.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
The AI Review Lottery: Widespread AI-Assisted Peer Reviews Boost Paper
  Scores and Acceptance Rates
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Journals and conferences worry that peer reviews assisted by artificial
intelligence (AI), in particular, large language models (LLMs), may negatively
influence the validity and fairness of the peer-review system, a cornerstone of
modern science. In this work, we address this concern with a quasi-experimental
study of the prevalence and impact of AI-assisted peer reviews in the context
of the 2024 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), a
large and prestigious machine-learning conference. Our contributions are
threefold. Firstly, we obtain a lower bound for the prevalence of AI-assisted
reviews at ICLR 2024 using the GPTZero LLM detector, estimating that at least
$15.8\%$ of reviews were written with AI assistance. Secondly, we estimate the
impact of AI-assisted reviews on submission scores. Considering pairs of
reviews with different scores assigned to the same paper, we find that in
$53.4\%$ of pairs the AI-assisted review scores higher than the human review
($p = 0.002$; relative difference in probability of scoring higher: $+14.4\%$
in favor of AI-assisted reviews). Thirdly, we assess the impact of receiving an
AI-assisted peer review on submission acceptance. In a matched study,
submissions near the acceptance threshold that received an AI-assisted peer
review were $4.9$ percentage points ($p = 0.024$) more likely to be accepted
than submissions that did not. Overall, we show that AI-assisted reviews are
consequential to the peer-review process and offer a discussion on future
implications of current trends
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: This paper examines the prevalence and causal effects of AI-assisted (LLM-assisted) peer reviews within the ICLR 2024 conference. It quantifies that at least 15.8% of reviews were AI-assisted, demonstrates that AI-assisted reviews tend to assign higher scores compared to human reviews (with a 14.4% relative increase in probability of scoring higher), and shows via a matched study that these reviews increase acceptance rates (especially for borderline submissions) by up to 4.9 percentage points.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The study employs a quasi-experimental design using an LLM detector (GPTZero) to classify reviews as AI-assisted or human-written. It conducts three main analyses: (1) prevalence estimation using GPTZero across multiple years with adjustments for false positives; (2) pairwise score comparisons between AI-assisted and human reviews for the same paper using both average differences and proportional odds regression; (3) a matched study applying content-based matching and logistic regression to estimate the causal effect on paper acceptance.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The experimental setup is based on review and submission data from ICLR spanning 2018 to 2024 (with detailed analysis on the 2024 dataset comprising 28,028 reviews and 7,404 submissions). The paper uses the OpenReview API, applies statistical methods (bootstrap resampling, ordinal regression, logistic regression), and employs matching techniques (exact matching on review scores and content-based matching using Sentence-BERT) to control for confounding factors.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The study is limited to the ICLR conference where peer reviews are openly available, which might not generalize to other venues. It relies on the accuracy of the GPTZero detector and does not account for false negatives, meaning the prevalence estimates are lower bounds. Additionally, the analysis does not fully explore how AI tools are specifically used (e.g., as simple text enhancers vs. formulating core arguments) and assumes no hidden confounders in the matched study.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore detailed usage modes of LLM assistance in peer reviews, assess the quality and substantive differences between AI-assisted and human reviews, extend the analysis to other conferences and domains, investigate the long-term impacts on the peer review system and trust in science, and develop guidelines for integrating AI tools in the review process while mitigating potential biases.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Subtractive Mixture Models via Squaring: Representation and Learning
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Mixture models are traditionally represented and learned by adding several

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:

candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Journals and conferences worry that peer reviews assisted by artificial
intelligence (AI), in particular, large language models (LLMs), may negatively
influence the validity and fairness of the peer-review system, a cornerstone of
modern science. In this work, we address this concern with a quasi-experimental
study of the prevalence and impact of AI-assisted peer reviews in the context
of the 2024 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), a
large and prestigious machine-learning conference. Our contributions are
threefold. Firstly, we obtain a lower bound for the prevalence of AI-assisted
reviews at ICLR 2024 using the GPTZero LLM detector, estimating that at least
$15.8\%$ of reviews were written with AI assistance. Secondly, we estimate the
impact of AI-assisted reviews on submission scores. Considering pairs of
reviews with different scores assigned to the same paper, we find that in
$53.4\%$ of pairs the AI-assisted review scores higher than the human review
($p = 0.002$; relative difference in probability of scoring higher: $+14.4\%$
in favor of AI-assisted reviews). Thirdly, we assess the impact of receiving an

submissions near the acceptance threshold that received an AI-assisted peer
review were $4.9$ percentage points ($p = 0.024$) more likely to be accepted
than submissions that did not. Overall, we show that AI-assisted reviews are
consequential to the peer-review process and offer a discussion on future
implications of current trends

Ordinal regression and logistic regression models are used to estimate the causal effects on paper scores and acceptance rates.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Data from ICLR submissions and reviews (from 2018 to 2024) are used, with a detailed focus on the 2024 conference data. The dataset includes thousands of submissions and reviews. Validation is conducted via bootstrapping, sensitivity analyses (varying the detection threshold of GPTZero), and matched pair comparisons to ensure robustness. Benchmarks include score differences and acceptance probabilities across similar papers.

The AI Review Lottery: Widespread AI-Assisted Peer Reviews Boost Paper
  Scores and Acceptance Rates
selected_add_paper_info_list.summary:
Journals and conferences worry that peer reviews assisted by artificial
intelligence (AI), in particular, large language models (LLMs), may negatively
influence the validity and fairness of the peer-review system, a cornerstone of
modern science. In this work, we address this concern with a quasi-experimental
study of the prevalence and impact of AI-assisted peer reviews in the context
of the 2024 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), a
large and prestigious machine-learning conference. Our contributions are
threefold. Firstly, we obtain a lower bound for the prevalence of AI-assisted
reviews at ICLR 2024 using the GPTZero LLM detector, estimating that at least
$15.8\%$ of reviews were written with AI assistance. Secondly, we estimate the
impact of AI-assisted reviews on submission scores. Considering pairs of
reviews with different scores assigned to the same paper, we find that in
$53.4\%$ of pairs the AI-assisted review scores higher than the human review
($p = 0.002$; relative difference in probability of scoring higher: $+14.4\%$
in favor of AI-assisted reviews). Thirdly, we assess the impact of receiving an
AI-assisted peer review on submission acceptance. In a matched study,
submissions near the acceptance threshold that received an AI-assisted peer
review were $4.9$ percentage points ($p = 0.024$) more likely to be accepted
than submissions that did not. Overall, we show that AI-assisted reviews are
consequential to the peer-review process and offer a discussion on future
implications of current trends
selected_add_paper_info_list.main_contributions: This paper examines the prevalence and causal effects of AI-assisted (LLM-assisted) peer reviews within the ICLR 2024 conference. It quantifies that at least 15.8% of reviews were AI-assisted, demonstrates that AI-assisted reviews tend to assign higher scores compared to human reviews (with a 14.4% relative increase in probability of scoring higher), and shows via a matched study that these reviews increase acceptance rates (especially for borderline submissions) by up to 4.9 percentage points.
selected_add_paper_info_list.methodology: The study employs a quasi-experimental design using an LLM detector (GPTZero) to classify reviews as AI-assisted or human-written. It conducts three main analyses: (1) prevalence estimation using GPTZero across multiple years with adjustments for false positives; (2) pairwise score comparisons between AI-assisted and human reviews for the same paper using both average differences and proportional odds regression; (3) a matched study applying content-based matching and logistic regression to estimate the causal effect on paper acceptance.
selected_add_paper_info_list.experimental_setup: The experimental setup is based on review and submission data from ICLR spanning 2018 to 2024 (with detailed analysis on the 2024 dataset comprising 28,028 reviews and 7,404 submissions). The paper uses the OpenReview API, applies statistical methods (bootstrap resampling, ordinal regression, logistic regression), and employs matching techniques (exact matching on review scores and content-based matching using Sentence-BERT) to control for confounding factors.
selected_add_paper_info_list.limitations: The study is limited to the ICLR conference where peer reviews are openly available, which might not generalize to other venues. It relies on the accuracy of the GPTZero detector and does not account for false negatives, meaning the prevalence estimates are lower bounds. Additionally, the analysis does not fully explore how AI tools are specifically used (e.g., as simple text enhancers vs. formulating core arguments) and assumes no hidden confounders in the matched study.
selected_add_paper_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore detailed usage modes of LLM assistance in peer reviews, assess the quality and substantive differences between AI-assisted and human reviews, extend the analysis to other conferences and domains, investigate the long-term impacts on the peer review system and trust in science, and develop guidelines for integrating AI tools in the review process while mitigating potential biases.

selected_add_paper_info_list.summary:

represent tensorized mixtures and generalize several other subtractive models.

can be exponentially more expressive than traditional additive mixtures; and,
we empirically show this increased expressiveness on a series of real-world
distribution estimation tasks.
selected_add_paper_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a novel framework for representing and learning subtractive (non-monotonic) mixture models via squaring within the framework of tensorized probabilistic circuits (PCs), dubbed NPC2s. Evaluation metrics include log-likelihoods on training and test data alongside computational efficiency measurements.

McFarland","James Y. Zou"],"published_date":"2024-03-11T21:51:39Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"We present an approach for estimating the fraction of text in a large corpus
which is likely to be substantially modified or produced by a large language
model (LLM). Our maximum likelihood model leverages expert-written and
AI-generated reference texts to accurately and efficiently examine real-world
LLM-use at the corpus level. We apply this approach to a case study of
scientific peer review in AI conferences that took place after the release of
ChatGPT: ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023. Our results suggest
that between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these
conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs, i.e. beyond
spell-checking or minor writing updates. The circumstances in which generated
text occurs offer insight into user behavior: the estimated fraction of
LLM-generated text is higher in reviews which report lower confidence, were
submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to
respond to author rebuttals. We also observe corpus-level trends in generated
text which may be too subtle to detect at the individual level, and discuss the
implications of such trends on peer review. We call for future
interdisciplinary work to examine how LLM use is changing our information and
knowledge practices.","github_url":"https://github.com/Weixin-Liang/Mapping-the-Increasing-Use-of-LLMs-in-Scientific-Papers","main_contributions":"The paper introduces a computationally efficient framework to estimate the fraction (α) of AI-modified text in large corpora, specifically focusing on academic peer reviews. By modeling the review corpus as a mixture of human-written and AI-generated texts using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), the method is applied to evaluate changes in review quality and style post-ChatGPT release across major machine learning conferences.","methodology":"The approach leverages historical data to create two reference distributions (P for human-written and Q for AI-generated texts) using token occurrence statistics (with a focus on adjectives, among other parts of speech). A mixture model is then established as (1 − α)P + αQ and maximum likelihood estimation is used to determine the fraction α. The methodology includes validation on synthetic mixtures and theoretical analysis showing the robustness and efficiency of the estimation.","experimental_setup":"Experiments were conducted on peer review datasets from major ML conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, EMNLP) as well as Nature portfolio journals. The setup involved generating AI-modified texts using LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 Chat, and Claude-2.1), creating synthetic mixtures with known proportions of AI-generated content, and comparing the MLE-based estimation against other instance-based detection methods. Extensive validation using bootstrap sampling and comparisons to baseline classifiers were performed, along with stratified analysis based on factors like submission deadlines and presence of scholarly citations.","limitations":"The framework primarily focuses on detecting modifications from ChatGPT and similar models, which may not capture the full diversity of LLM outputs. It relies on simplifying assumptions such as representing documents based on token occurrence (e.g., adjectives) and may be sensitive to changes in style or prompt variations. Moreover, approximations in modeling the mixture and dependency on historical training data could introduce estimation errors and may not account for all nuances in human vs. AI writing styles.","future_research_directions":"Future work could extend the framework to additional domains and other forms of AI-generated content beyond peer reviews, refine the methodology by incorporating different token types and deeper linguistic features, and address ethical and privacy concerns in using peer review data. There is also scope to improve robustness against prompt shifts, to explore fine-grained analysis at the document level, and to study long-term impacts on review quality and diversity in scholarly communication."}

Below is the outcome of step 3—a novel method inspired by the Base Method and one of the Add Method approaches:

────────────────────────────
Proposed Method: Subtractive Transformer Enhanced Mixture (STEM)
────────────────────────────

Overview:
STEM is a fundamentally new approach for detecting and quantifying AI-assisted modifications in large text corpora. It combines the idea of mixture modeling from the Base Method with the expressive power and “subtractive” mechanism from recent advances in subtractive mixture models. Critically, STEM departs from simple token‐frequency statistics by leveraging deep, learned text representations and allowing for negative “subtractive” interactions that cancel shared stylistic features between human-written and AI-generated texts.

How STEM Works:
1. Deep Representation Extraction:
 • Instead of relying on handcrafted features like adjective counts, input texts are mapped into high-dimensional semantic embeddings using a pre-trained transformer encoder (tuned on domain-specific texts).
 • This encoder produces rich representations that capture nuanced language patterns, including style, tone, and context.

2. Subtractive Mixture Modeling:
 • Two components are defined: one for human-written content (Pₕ) and one for AI-generated text (Qₐᵢ). Unlike traditional additive mixtures, STEM models the observed text distribution as a subtractive mixture.
 • Specifically, the model represents document density as the square of a (potentially subtractive) mixture:
   f(x) = [ (1 – α) gₕ(x) – α gₐᵢ(x) ]²
 where gₕ and gₐᵢ are neural networks mapping embeddings to “style scores” (which can be positive or negative), and the squaring guarantees non-negativity.
 • This subtraction captures the idea that certain stylistic signals are common to both human and AI texts; by “canceling out” these overlapping traits, the model focuses on differences that distinguish AI assistance. In effect, the subtractive mechanism improves sensitivity to subtle shifts—such as modifications made only beyond routine editing—addressing the Base Method’s limitation of oversimplified token statistics.

3. Joint Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Fine-Tuning:
 • STEM is trained end-to-end using maximum likelihood. The mixture weight α (denoting the fraction of AI-assisted content) is estimated simultaneously with the parameters of gₕ and gₐᵢ.
 • An auxiliary loss (or regularizer) is added to encourage alignment with contextual metadata (e.g., submission timing, reviewer confidence) so that the method adapts to trends like near-deadline modifications.
 • In practice, this results in a flexible model that not only outputs corpus-level estimates of AI influence but also yields document-level probabilities—helping to flag reviews or articles falling on the ambiguous border between human and AI style.

4. Robustness and Adaptation:
 • By using learned embeddings, STEM is more robust to changes in LLM prompt behavior, style shifts over time, and variations across domains.
 • The subtractive structure, inspired by the “Subtractive Mixture Models via Squaring” approach, increases expressiveness—allowing the method to model complex interactions between latent stylistic factors.

Benefits Over the Base Method:
 • Richer representations replace simple adjective/token counts, addressing the oversimplification.
 • The subtractive (squared) mixture provides enhanced expressiveness allowing cancellation of overlapping features, making the detection less sensitive to prompt variations.
 • Joint training with auxiliary metadata results in an adaptable framework that can adjust as AI-assisted writing evolves.
 • STEM enables both aggregate (corpus-level α) and individual-level detections, offering fine-grained insights unavailable in the original Base Method.

Conclusion:
STEM represents a genuinely new method that leverages deep representations alongside subtractive mixture modeling. It mitigates challenges of style sensitivity and simplistic feature selection in the Base Method, offering a robust, adaptive, and nuanced tool for quantifying and analyzing AI-assisted texts across large-scale corpora.

1. Controlled Synthetic Dataset Experiment

Objective:

 • Train and compare two mixture models:
  – STEM using a subtractive mixture mechanism  
  – A baseline additive mixture model (Base Method)  
 • Evaluate using performance metrics such as mean squared error (MSE) for α estimation and document-level classification accuracy.

Experimental Setup:
 A. Data Generation
  1. Start with a collection of annotated human text samples.
  2. For each sample, create an “AI-assisted” version by simulating changes (e.g., style changes, vocabulary alterations) or using an AI text generator with preset parameters.
  3. For each synthetic document, assign a ground truth α (e.g., 0 ≤ α ≤ 1) representing the proportion of AI modifications.

 B. Feature Extraction
  – Use HuggingFace pretrained transformers (e.g., RoBERTa or BERT) to extract embeddings:
   • Leverage the pipeline “feature-extraction” to convert text into representations.
   • Optionally fine-tune the embedding extractor on a subset of data if required.

 C. Model Definitions in PyTorch
  – Define two networks:
   1. gₕ(x): Responsibility network for human text features.
   2. gₐᵢ(x): Network capturing AI-assisted modifications.
  – For STEM, implement the subtractive mechanism as:
    f(x) = [ (1 – α) * gₕ(x) – α * gₐᵢ(x) ]²
   • The Base Method simply uses an additive combination (e.g., f(x) = gₕ(x) + gₐᵢ(x) or a weighted sum without subtraction).

 D. Training and Evaluation
  – Use synthetic ground truth α values to compute the regression loss (mean squared error).
  – At the document level, threshold the output to classify whether a document is predominantly AI-assisted vs. human.
  – Log training curves and compare performance (accuracy and MSE) between STEM and the additive model across a range of α values.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import numpy as np

# Loading a pretrained transformer model and tokenizer for feature extraction.
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer.eval()  # disable dropout, etc.

def extract_embeddings(text):
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model_transformer(**inputs)
    # Use the [CLS] token output or mean pooling of last hidden states
    embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
    return embeddings

# Define network modules for g_h and g_ai using PyTorch.
class FeatureExtractor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super(FeatureExtractor, self).__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(self.fc(x))

# Example STEM model with subtractive mechanism.
class STEMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(STEMModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)  # assuming 768-dim from RoBERTa
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
    
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        # alpha is assumed to be provided as a tensor of shape [batch_size, 1]
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # Subtractive mixture: computing squared difference component-wise.
        mixed = ( (1 - alpha) * human_features - alpha * ai_features ) ** 2
        # Sum or mean the squared differences to produce a scalar score.
        return mixed.mean(dim=1)

# Training loop outline

        loss = criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))  # target 0 for correct mixture alignment

   • Combine the human and AI features additively.

   • Same as Variant 1 but add an auxiliary loss term, e.g. L_aux = || predicted_metadata - true_metadata ||².
  Variant 3: Full STEM with Subtractive Mixture
   • Incorporate the subtractive mixture mechanism described in Experiment 1 and include the metadata regularizer.

 C. Loss Functions and Training
  – For each variant, define:
   • A primary loss (e.g., MSE or cross-entropy for document-level classification)
   • An auxiliary metadata loss for variants 2 and 3.
  – Use a common training loop to ensure that any differences in convergence behavior are due solely to the model architecture.

--------------------------------------------------
class AdditiveModel(nn.Module):
    """Pure additive model without metadata."""
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(AdditiveModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)

    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # Simple additive model: weighted sum.
        mixed = (1 - alpha) * human_features + alpha * ai_features
        return mixed.mean(dim=1)

class AdditiveWithMetadataModel(AdditiveModel):
    """Additive model with auxiliary metadata loss."""
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, metadata_dim):
        super(AdditiveWithMetadataModel, self).__init__(hidden_dim)
        self.metadata_predictor = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, metadata_dim)
        
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        mixed_features = super().forward(embeddings, alpha)
        # Predict metadata properties from mixed features.
        metadata_pred = self.metadata_predictor(mixed_features.unsqueeze(1))
        return mixed_features, metadata_pred

# Custom training step accommodating auxiliary loss.
def train_variant(model, data_loader, optimizer, primary_criterion, aux_criterion=None, lambda_aux=0.5):
    model.train()
    for text, true_alpha, true_metadata in data_loader:
        embeddings = extract_embeddings(text)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        if isinstance(model, AdditiveWithMetadataModel) or hasattr(model, 'metadata_predictor'):
            outputs, metadata_pred = model(embeddings, true_alpha.view(-1, 1))
            primary_loss = primary_criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))
            aux_loss = aux_criterion(metadata_pred, true_metadata)
            loss = primary_loss + lambda_aux * aux_loss
        else:
            outputs = model(embeddings, true_alpha.view(-1, 1))
            loss = primary_criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
--------------------------------------------------

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import numpy as np
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, accuracy_score
import seaborn as sns
import random

# Set random seeds for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)

##############################################
# 1. Helper Functions and Model Definitions  #
##############################################

# Load a pretrained transformer model and its tokenizer for feature extraction.
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer.eval()  # set to eval mode as dropout is not needed

def extract_embeddings(text_list):
    """
    Extract embeddings for a list of texts using the pretrained transformer.
    Uses mean pooling over the last hidden state.
    Returns a tensor of shape (batch_size, embedding_dim)
    """
    inputs = tokenizer(text_list, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model_transformer(**inputs)
    embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
    return embeddings

class FeatureExtractor(nn.Module):
    """Simple fully connected layer with ReLU for feature projection."""
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super(FeatureExtractor, self).__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(self.fc(x))

# STEM Model: Uses subtractive mixture mechanism.
class STEMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(STEMModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)  # 768 from roberta-base embeddings
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
    
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        # alpha assumed tensor shape: [batch_size, 1]
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        mixed = ((1 - alpha) * human_features - alpha * ai_features) ** 2
        # average squared differences as the output scalar per sample
        out = mixed.mean(dim=1)
        return out

# Base Additive Model: Uses additive mechanism.
class AdditiveModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(AdditiveModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)

    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # weighted additive mix
        mixed = (1 - alpha) * human_features + alpha * ai_features
        # average as an aggregate feature score
        out = mixed.mean(dim=1)
        return out

# Additive Model with Auxiliary Metadata Loss.
class AdditiveWithMetadataModel(AdditiveModel):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, metadata_dim):
        super(AdditiveWithMetadataModel, self).__init__(hidden_dim)
        self.metadata_predictor = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, metadata_dim)

        mixed_feature = super().forward(embeddings, alpha)

        # In practice, one would tap into the layer before averaging.
        metadata_pred = self.metadata_predictor(mixed_feature.unsqueeze(1))

    texts = []
    alphas = []
    for i in range(num_samples):
        # simulate a human text sample and an AI-assisted modification pattern.
        base_text = f"This is sample text number {i} written by a human."
        # Simulate AI change by appending a phrase. In practice, modifications could be more subtle.
        ai_text = base_text + " With AI modifications."
        # Randomly combine the two; alpha indicates proportion of AI assistance.
        alpha = np.round(np.random.uniform(0, 1), 2)
        # For simplicity, choose one of the versions based on alpha threshold.
        text = base_text if alpha < 0.5 else ai_text
        texts.append(text)
        alphas.append(torch.tensor(alpha, dtype=torch.float32))
    return list(zip(texts, alphas))

def generate_metadata_data(num_samples=10, metadata_dim=1):
    """
    Generate synthetic data for Experiment 2.
    Each sample is a tuple: (text, true_alpha, true_metadata)
    Here, metadata is simulated as a single number.
    """
    data = []
    for i in range(num_samples):
        base_text = f"Document {i}: Analysis of human vs AI writing."
        ai_text = base_text + " Including AI stylistic changes."
        alpha = np.round(np.random.uniform(0, 1), 2)
        text = base_text if alpha < 0.5 else ai_text
        # For demonstration, simulate metadata as a function of alpha plus some noise.
        metadata = torch.tensor([alpha + np.random.normal(0, 0.1)], dtype=torch.float32)
        data.append((text, torch.tensor(alpha, dtype=torch.float32), metadata))
    return data

def generate_domain_data(num_samples=20):
    """
    Generate synthetic domain-specific data for Experiment 3.
    Each sample is a tuple: (text, true_alpha, true_metadata, domain_label)
    Two domains: 'news' and 'academic'
    """
    data = []
    for i in range(num_samples):
        # Alternate domains roughly equally.
        domain = "news" if i % 2 == 0 else "academic"
        base_text = f"{domain.capitalize()} article {i}: This is a text sample."
        ai_text = base_text + " With additional AI enhancements."
        alpha = np.round(np.random.uniform(0, 1), 2)
        text = base_text if alpha < 0.5 else ai_text
        # Simulated metadata (not used in evaluation but for demonstration)
        metadata = torch.tensor([alpha + np.random.normal(0, 0.05)], dtype=torch.float32)
        data.append((text, torch.tensor(alpha, dtype=torch.float32), metadata, domain))
    return data

##########################################
# 3. Training and Evaluation Utilities   #
##########################################

def train_model(model, data, num_epochs=5, lr=1e-3, use_metadata=False):
    """
    Training loop for a given model over synthetic data.
    data: list of tuples.
      - For Experiment 1: (text, true_alpha)
      - For Experiment 2: (text, true_alpha, true_metadata)
    Returns loss_history (list of loss values per epoch).
    """
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    lambda_aux = 0.5  # weight for metadata auxiliary loss if used
    loss_history = []

    print("Starting training for {} epochs...".format(num_epochs))
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        epoch_losses = []
        for sample in data:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            # unpack sample
            if use_metadata:
                text, true_alpha, true_metadata = sample
            else:
                text, true_alpha = sample

            embeddings = extract_embeddings([text])  # batch size 1
            alpha_tensor = true_alpha.view(-1, 1)
            if use_metadata and hasattr(model, 'metadata_predictor'):
                output, metadata_pred = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
                primary_loss = criterion(output, torch.zeros_like(output))
                aux_loss = criterion(metadata_pred, true_metadata)
                loss = primary_loss + lambda_aux * aux_loss
            else:
                output = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
                loss = criterion(output, torch.zeros_like(output))
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            epoch_losses.append(loss.item())
        avg_loss = np.mean(epoch_losses)
        loss_history.append(avg_loss)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{num_epochs} - Loss: {avg_loss:.4f}")
    return loss_history

def evaluate_model(model, data):
    """
    Evaluate model over provided data.
    Assumes data is of the form (text, true_alpha, ...)
    Returns MSE between model output and zero (dummy target) as demonstration.
    """
    pred_list = []
    true_list = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for sample in data:
            # accommodating both with or without metadata/domaind
            text = sample[0]
            true_alpha = sample[1]
            embeddings = extract_embeddings([text])
            alpha_tensor = true_alpha.view(-1, 1)
            output = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
            pred_list.append(output.item())
            true_list.append(0.0)  # dummy true target for demonstration
    mse_val = mean_squared_error(true_list, pred_list)
    print("Evaluation MSE: {:.4f}".format(mse_val))
    return mse_val

def plot_training_curve(loss_history, figure_topic="training_loss", condition=None, pair=None):
    """
    Plot the training loss curve using matplotlib and save as .pdf
    """
    plt.figure()
    epochs = list(range(1, len(loss_history)+1))
    sns.lineplot(x=epochs, y=loss_history, marker="o")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Loss")
    title = "Training Loss"
    if condition is not None:
        title += f" ({condition})"
    plt.title(title)
    filename = figure_topic
    if condition is not None:
        filename += f"_{condition}"
    if pair is not None:
        filename += f"_pair{pair}"
    filename += ".pdf"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(filename)
    print(f"Saved training curve as {filename}")
    plt.close()  # close figure

###############################################
# 4. Experiment 1: Controlled Synthetic Dataset #
###############################################

def experiment_controlled_synthetic():
    print("\nExperiment 1: Controlled Synthetic Dataset Experiment")
    data = generate_synthetic_data(num_samples=10)
    # Initialize STEM model (using subtractive mixture) and a baseline additive model.
    stem_model = STEMModel(hidden_dim=128)
    baseline_model = AdditiveModel(hidden_dim=128)
    
    # For demonstration, perform few epochs of training on dummy data.
    print("Training STEM model...")
    stem_loss_history = train_model(stem_model, data, num_epochs=3)
    print("Training Baseline Additive model...")
    baseline_loss_history = train_model(baseline_model, data, num_epochs=3)
    
    # Plot training curves
    plot_training_curve(stem_loss_history, figure_topic="training_loss", condition="STEM", pair=1)
    plot_training_curve(baseline_loss_history, figure_topic="training_loss", condition="baseline", pair=2)

    # Evaluate models (here using dummy evaluation, as target is 0)
    print("Evaluating STEM model:")
    evaluate_model(stem_model, data)
    print("Evaluating Baseline model:")
    evaluate_model(baseline_model, data)

###############################################
# 5. Experiment 2: Ablation Study on Subtractive Mechanism and Metadata #
###############################################

def experiment_ablation_study():
    print("\nExperiment 2: Ablation Study on Subtractive Mechanism and Auxiliary Metadata")
    data = generate_metadata_data(num_samples=10, metadata_dim=1)
    
    # Variant 1: Pure Additive Model (without metadata)
    additive_model = AdditiveModel(hidden_dim=128)
    # Variant 2: Additive with Metadata
    additive_meta_model = AdditiveWithMetadataModel(hidden_dim=128, metadata_dim=1)
    # Variant 3: Full STEM with Metadata (STEM model is not originally built with metadata;
    # for demonstration, we just use STEMModel and compute auxiliary loss on dummy metadata).
    # We simulate metadata integration by adding a metadata predictor to STEM.
    class STEMWithMetadataModel(STEMModel):
        def __init__(self, hidden_dim, metadata_dim):
            super(STEMWithMetadataModel, self).__init__(hidden_dim)
            self.metadata_predictor = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, metadata_dim)
        def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
            human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
            ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
            mixed = ((1 - alpha) * human_features - alpha * ai_features) ** 2
            # get aggregated feature before mean (simulate by taking human_features here)
            feature_repr = human_features  # dummy representation
            output = mixed.mean(dim=1)
            metadata_pred = self.metadata_predictor(feature_repr)
            return output, metadata_pred

    stem_meta_model = STEMWithMetadataModel(hidden_dim=128, metadata_dim=1)
    
    # Train each variant for a few epochs.
    print("Training Pure Additive Model (Variant 1)...")
    loss_additive = train_model(additive_model, data, num_epochs=3, use_metadata=False)
    print("Training Additive with Metadata Model (Variant 2)...")
    loss_additive_meta = train_model(additive_meta_model, data, num_epochs=3, use_metadata=True)
    print("Training Full STEM with Metadata Model (Variant 3)...")
    loss_stem_meta = train_model(stem_meta_model, data, num_epochs=3, use_metadata=True)
    
    # Plot training curves for all three variants.
    plot_training_curve(loss_additive, figure_topic="training_loss", condition="additive", pair=1)
    plot_training_curve(loss_additive_meta, figure_topic="training_loss", condition="additive_meta", pair=2)
    plot_training_curve(loss_stem_meta, figure_topic="training_loss", condition="STEM_meta", pair=3)
    
    # Evaluation (dummy targets)
    print("Evaluating Variant 1 (Pure Additive):")
    evaluate_model(additive_model, data)
    print("Evaluating Variant 2 (Additive with Metadata):")
    # For variants with metadata, only evaluate primary output.
    def evaluate_model_with_metadata(model, data):
        pred_list = []
        with torch.no_grad():
            for sample in data:
                text = sample[0]
                true_alpha = sample[1]
                embeddings = extract_embeddings([text])
                alpha_tensor = true_alpha.view(-1, 1)
                if hasattr(model, 'metadata_predictor'):
                    output, _ = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
                else:
                    output = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
                pred_list.append(output.item())
        mse_val = mean_squared_error([0.0]*len(pred_list), pred_list)
        print("Evaluation MSE: {:.4f}".format(mse_val))
        return mse_val
    evaluate_model_with_metadata(additive_meta_model, data)
    print("Evaluating Variant 3 (Full STEM with Metadata):")
    evaluate_model_with_metadata(stem_meta_model, data)

###############################################
# 6. Experiment 3: Robustness Under Domain Shifts  #
###############################################

def experiment_domain_shift():
    print("\nExperiment 3: Robustness Under Domain Shifts")
    data = generate_domain_data(num_samples=20)
    # Split data based on domain: use all non-'academic' as training and 'academic' as testing.
    train_data = [sample for sample in data if sample[-1] != "academic"]
    test_data = [sample for sample in data if sample[-1] == "academic"]
    print("Training samples:", len(train_data), " | Testing samples:", len(test_data))
    
    # For demonstration, we use STEMModel as our method.
    domain_model = STEMModel(hidden_dim=128)
    print("Training STEM model on non-academic domain...")
    train_model(domain_model, train_data, num_epochs=3)
    
    print("Evaluating model on academic domain (domain shift)...")
    mse_val = evaluate_model(domain_model, test_data)
    
    # Plot domain evaluation: for demonstration, plot prediction scatter (dummy targets vs predictions)
    predictions = []
    targets = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for sample in test_data:
            text = sample[0]
            true_alpha = sample[1]
            embeddings = extract_embeddings([text])
            alpha_tensor = true_alpha.view(-1, 1)
            output = domain_model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
            predictions.append(output.item())
            targets.append(0.0)  # dummy target
    plt.figure()
    sns.scatterplot(x=targets, y=predictions)
    plt.xlabel("True Value (dummy zero)")
    plt.ylabel("Predicted Value")
    plt.title("Domain Shift Predictions (Academic)")
    filename = "inference_latency_domain_pair1.pdf"
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(filename)
    print(f"Saved domain shift scatter plot as {filename}")
    plt.close()

###############################################
# 7. Test Function to Validate Code Execution #
###############################################

def run_tests():
    """
    Run a quick test that executes each experiment with a very small dataset and few epochs.
    This function is intended to complete immediately.
    """
    print("\nRunning quick tests for all experiments...")
    experiment_controlled_synthetic()
    experiment_ablation_study()
    experiment_domain_shift()
    print("\nAll tests finished successfully.")

###############################################
# Main: Run tests if executed as a script
###############################################

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_tests()

    new_method: Below is the outcome of step 3—a novel method inspired by the Base Method and one of the Add Method approaches:

────────────────────────────
Proposed Method: Subtractive Transformer Enhanced Mixture (STEM)
────────────────────────────

Overview:
STEM is a fundamentally new approach for detecting and quantifying AI-assisted modifications in large text corpora. It combines the idea of mixture modeling from the Base Method with the expressive power and “subtractive” mechanism from recent advances in subtractive mixture models. Critically, STEM departs from simple token‐frequency statistics by leveraging deep, learned text representations and allowing for negative “subtractive” interactions that cancel shared stylistic features between human-written and AI-generated texts.

How STEM Works:
1. Deep Representation Extraction:
 • Instead of relying on handcrafted features like adjective counts, input texts are mapped into high-dimensional semantic embeddings using a pre-trained transformer encoder (tuned on domain-specific texts).
 • This encoder produces rich representations that capture nuanced language patterns, including style, tone, and context.

2. Subtractive Mixture Modeling:
 • Two components are defined: one for human-written content (Pₕ) and one for AI-generated text (Qₐᵢ). Unlike traditional additive mixtures, STEM models the observed text distribution as a subtractive mixture.
 • Specifically, the model represents document density as the square of a (potentially subtractive) mixture:
   f(x) = [ (1 – α) gₕ(x) – α gₐᵢ(x) ]²
 where gₕ and gₐᵢ are neural networks mapping embeddings to “style scores” (which can be positive or negative), and the squaring guarantees non-negativity.
 • This subtraction captures the idea that certain stylistic signals are common to both human and AI texts; by “canceling out” these overlapping traits, the model focuses on differences that distinguish AI assistance. In effect, the subtractive mechanism improves sensitivity to subtle shifts—such as modifications made only beyond routine editing—addressing the Base Method’s limitation of oversimplified token statistics.

3. Joint Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Fine-Tuning:
 • STEM is trained end-to-end using maximum likelihood. The mixture weight α (denoting the fraction of AI-assisted content) is estimated simultaneously with the parameters of gₕ and gₐᵢ.
 • An auxiliary loss (or regularizer) is added to encourage alignment with contextual metadata (e.g., submission timing, reviewer confidence) so that the method adapts to trends like near-deadline modifications.
 • In practice, this results in a flexible model that not only outputs corpus-level estimates of AI influence but also yields document-level probabilities—helping to flag reviews or articles falling on the ambiguous border between human and AI style.

4. Robustness and Adaptation:
 • By using learned embeddings, STEM is more robust to changes in LLM prompt behavior, style shifts over time, and variations across domains.
 • The subtractive structure, inspired by the “Subtractive Mixture Models via Squaring” approach, increases expressiveness—allowing the method to model complex interactions between latent stylistic factors.

Benefits Over the Base Method:
 • Richer representations replace simple adjective/token counts, addressing the oversimplification.
 • The subtractive (squared) mixture provides enhanced expressiveness allowing cancellation of overlapping features, making the detection less sensitive to prompt variations.
 • Joint training with auxiliary metadata results in an adaptable framework that can adjust as AI-assisted writing evolves.
 • STEM enables both aggregate (corpus-level α) and individual-level detections, offering fine-grained insights unavailable in the original Base Method.

Conclusion:
STEM represents a genuinely new method that leverages deep representations alongside subtractive mixture modeling. It mitigates challenges of style sensitivity and simplistic feature selection in the Base Method, offering a robust, adaptive, and nuanced tool for quantifying and analyzing AI-assisted texts across large-scale corpora.

 • Use controlled modifications (either by deterministic changes or by running parts of texts through an AI generator with known parameters) so that the ground truth mixture weight (α) is available.  
 • Train and compare two mixture models:
  – STEM using a subtractive mixture mechanism  
  – A baseline additive mixture model (Base Method)  
 • Evaluate using performance metrics such as mean squared error (MSE) for α estimation and document-level classification accuracy.

Experimental Setup:
 A. Data Generation
  1. Start with a collection of annotated human text samples.
  2. For each sample, create an “AI-assisted” version by simulating changes (e.g., style changes, vocabulary alterations) or using an AI text generator with preset parameters.
  3. For each synthetic document, assign a ground truth α (e.g., 0 ≤ α ≤ 1) representing the proportion of AI modifications.

 B. Feature Extraction

   • Leverage the pipeline “feature-extraction” to convert text into representations.

 C. Model Definitions in PyTorch
  – Define two networks:
   1. gₕ(x): Responsibility network for human text features.
   2. gₐᵢ(x): Network capturing AI-assisted modifications.
  – For STEM, implement the subtractive mechanism as:
    f(x) = [ (1 – α) * gₕ(x) – α * gₐᵢ(x) ]²
   • The Base Method simply uses an additive combination (e.g., f(x) = gₕ(x) + gₐᵢ(x) or a weighted sum without subtraction).

 D. Training and Evaluation

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import numpy as np

# Loading a pretrained transformer model and tokenizer for feature extraction.
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer.eval()  # disable dropout, etc.

def extract_embeddings(text):
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model_transformer(**inputs)
    # Use the [CLS] token output or mean pooling of last hidden states
    embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
    return embeddings

# Define network modules for g_h and g_ai using PyTorch.
class FeatureExtractor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super(FeatureExtractor, self).__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(self.fc(x))

# Example STEM model with subtractive mechanism.
class STEMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(STEMModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)  # assuming 768-dim from RoBERTa
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
    
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        # alpha is assumed to be provided as a tensor of shape [batch_size, 1]
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # Subtractive mixture: computing squared difference component-wise.
        mixed = ( (1 - alpha) * human_features - alpha * ai_features ) ** 2
        # Sum or mean the squared differences to produce a scalar score.
        return mixed.mean(dim=1)

# Training loop outline

        outputs = model(embeddings, alpha_tensor)
        loss = criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))  # target 0 for correct mixture alignment
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

class AdditiveModel(nn.Module):
    """Pure additive model without metadata."""
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(AdditiveModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)

    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # Simple additive model: weighted sum.
        mixed = (1 - alpha) * human_features + alpha * ai_features
        return mixed.mean(dim=1)

class AdditiveWithMetadataModel(AdditiveModel):
    """Additive model with auxiliary metadata loss."""
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, metadata_dim):
        super(AdditiveWithMetadataModel, self).__init__(hidden_dim)
        self.metadata_predictor = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, metadata_dim)
        
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        mixed_features = super().forward(embeddings, alpha)
        # Predict metadata properties from mixed features.
        metadata_pred = self.metadata_predictor(mixed_features.unsqueeze(1))
        return mixed_features, metadata_pred

# Custom training step accommodating auxiliary loss.
def train_variant(model, data_loader, optimizer, primary_criterion, aux_criterion=None, lambda_aux=0.5):
    model.train()
    for text, true_alpha, true_metadata in data_loader:
        embeddings = extract_embeddings(text)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        if isinstance(model, AdditiveWithMetadataModel) or hasattr(model, 'metadata_predictor'):
            outputs, metadata_pred = model(embeddings, true_alpha.view(-1, 1))
            primary_loss = primary_criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))
            aux_loss = aux_criterion(metadata_pred, true_metadata)
            loss = primary_loss + lambda_aux * aux_loss
        else:
            outputs = model(embeddings, true_alpha.view(-1, 1))
            loss = primary_criterion(outputs, torch.zeros_like(outputs))
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

"""
Required Python libraries:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import numpy as np
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, accuracy_score
import seaborn as sns
import random

# Set random seeds for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)
random.seed(42)

##############################################
# 1. Helper Functions and Model Definitions  #
##############################################

# Load a pretrained transformer model and its tokenizer for feature extraction.
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roberta-base")
model_transformer.eval()  # set to eval mode as dropout is not needed

def extract_embeddings(text_list):
    """
    Extract embeddings for a list of texts using the pretrained transformer.
    Uses mean pooling over the last hidden state.
    Returns a tensor of shape (batch_size, embedding_dim)
    """
    inputs = tokenizer(text_list, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model_transformer(**inputs)
    embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
    return embeddings

class FeatureExtractor(nn.Module):
    """Simple fully connected layer with ReLU for feature projection."""
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super(FeatureExtractor, self).__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(self.fc(x))

# STEM Model: Uses subtractive mixture mechanism.
class STEMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(STEMModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)  # 768 from roberta-base embeddings
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
    
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        # alpha assumed tensor shape: [batch_size, 1]
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        mixed = ((1 - alpha) * human_features - alpha * ai_features) ** 2
        # average squared differences as the output scalar per sample
        out = mixed.mean(dim=1)
        return out

# Base Additive Model: Uses additive mechanism.
class AdditiveModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super(AdditiveModel, self).__init__()
        self.g_h = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)
        self.g_ai = FeatureExtractor(768, hidden_dim)

    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        human_features = self.g_h(embeddings)
        ai_features = self.g_ai(embeddings)
        # weighted additive mix
        mixed = (1 - alpha) * human_features + alpha * ai_features
        # average as an aggregate feature score
        out = mixed.mean(dim=1)
        return out

# Additive Model with Auxiliary Metadata Loss.
class AdditiveWithMetadataModel(AdditiveModel):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, metadata_dim):
        super(AdditiveWithMetadataModel, self).__init__(hidden_dim)
        self.metadata_predictor = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, metadata_dim)
        
    def forward(self, embeddings, alpha):
        # get the mixed feature from the additive model
        mixed_feature = super().forward(embeddings, alpha)
        # reshape to [batch, hidden_dim] (simulate one-dimensional features here)
        # For demonstration, we treat the mixed_feature as having a dummy hidden_dim of size equal to 1.
        # In practice, one would tap into the layer before averaging.
        metadata_pred = self.metadata_predictor(mixed_feature.unsqueeze(1))
        return mixed_feature, metadata_pred
